content: Cystic fibrosis is a severe, life-threatening genetic disorder that primarily affects major organs, including the lungs and digestive system. Its management requires a complex and demanding daily treatment regimen, which typically includes airway clearance techniques, pancreatic enzyme supplementation, and various medications. However, adherence to this intensive treatment plan is often poor, particularly among adolescents. The chronic nature of the disease, combined with the burdensome treatment requirements, frequently results in a diminished quality of life for individuals with cystic fibrosis. There have been anecdotal reports suggesting that singing may serve as a beneficial adjunct therapy for individuals with cystic fibrosis. Singing is thought to provide exercise for the respiratory system while also offering a means of emotional expression, potentially improving overall quality of life. This review aimed to evaluate the effects of singing, when used alongside standard treatment, on quality of life, respiratory muscle strength, pulmonary function, and morbidity in children and adults with cystic fibrosis. To conduct this review, researchers searched multiple databases, including the Cystic Fibrosis Trials Register and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, with the most recent searches conducted in January and March 2019. They also reviewed clinical trial registries, conference proceedings, and relevant journals. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials comparing singing as an adjunct therapy to either a control intervention (e.g., playing computer games or engaging in craft activities) or no singing at all. Only one eligible randomized controlled trial was identified for analysis. This study, conducted in two pediatric hospitals in Australia, involved 40 participants with cystic fibrosis (mean age 11.6 years, 35% male). The trial compared the effects of an eight-session individual singing program to preferred recreational activities, such as playing computer games or watching movies. The study's small sample size (51 participants initially enrolled) and high dropout rate (21%) were significant limitations. The results showed no significant differences between the singing and control groups in terms of quality of life or respiratory function parameters immediately after the intervention or at follow-up. However, some improvements were observed in specific domains of the Cystic Fibrosis Questionnaire-Revised (e.g., emotional, social, and vitality domains) for both groups by the end of the treatment period. Regarding respiratory muscle strength, the singing group demonstrated a higher maximal expiratory pressure at follow-up (six to eight weeks post-intervention) compared to the control group, with a mean difference of 25.80 (95% confidence interval 5.94 to 45.66). No differences were observed between the groups for other respiratory function measures, such as maximal inspiratory pressure or spirometry results, at any time point. Importantly, no adverse effects were reported in the singing group, while adverse events in the control group were not documented in the study. In conclusion, the evidence from this review is insufficient to determine whether singing has a meaningful impact on quality of life or respiratory parameters in individuals with cystic fibrosis. Nonetheless, the findings highlight a growing interest in exploring non-medical, low-cost therapies for cystic fibrosis. Further research is warranted to investigate the potential benefits of singing on respiratory function and psychosocial well-being in this population.
